title: What am I running?
summary: Read /etc/os-release, uname, lsb_release and hostnamectl, and work out the family from ID and ID_LIKE.

steps.title: /etc/os-release
body: Every modern distro (systemd or not) ships `/etc/os-release`: shell-style `KEY=value` lines.
- `ID` is the distro, lowercase. `ID_LIKE` lists the distros it is **compatible with**, closest first (Rocky: `ID_LIKE="rhel centos fedora"`).
- Values may be quoted with `"` or `'`, or bare.
- Scripts use it like this: `. /etc/os-release; echo "$ID $VERSION_ID"`.

steps.prompt: Match the field to its value on Rocky Linux 9.4.

steps.title: The other commands
body: hostnamectl       Operating System: Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS, Kernel: ..., Architecture: ...
(systemd only; also shows virtualization: kvm, wsl, docker...)
lsb_release -a    Distributor ID / Description / Release / Codename
(needs the lsb-release package; often missing in containers)
In a container, `uname -r` shows the **host's** kernel (containers share it), while `/etc/os-release` shows the image's distro. Ask both questions separately.

steps.prompt: Inside an `alpine:3.20` container on an Ubuntu host, `uname -r` prints `6.8.0-45-generic`. Why?
options: Containers share the host kernel; only the userland comes from the image
steps.explain: That is the core difference between a container and a VM.

steps.prompt: Print the distro ID and version in a shell script.
steps.explain: Sourcing the file turns each line into a shell variable.

steps.title: Read os-release in a script
prompt: `/etc/os-release` is written in shell syntax on purpose, so a script can **source** it. Write `~/bin/osinfo` that
prints `ID VERSION_ID` (for example `debian 13`) for the file given as its argument, or for `/etc/os-release` when
there is none. Hosts without a `VERSION_ID` print `-` instead (`arch -`).
Source the file in a **subshell** (`( . "$f"; ... )`), so its variables (`NAME`, `VERSION`...) do not leak into the
rest of your script. Try it on `~/fleet/*/os-release`.

checks.name: osinfo with no argument reads /etc/os-release
checks.fail: `~/bin/osinfo` (no argument) should print `debian 13` here. Is it executable (`chmod +x`)?

checks.name: osinfo works on every fleet file
checks.cmd: for d in ~/fleet/*/; do want=$(ID= VERSION_ID=; . "$d/os-release"; echo "$ID ${VERSION_ID:--}"); got=$(~/bin/osinfo "$d/os-release" 2>/dev/null); [ "$got" = "$want" ] || { echo "$d: got '$got', want '$want'"; exit 1; }; done
checks.fail: One of the fleet files gives the wrong answer (below). Quotes around values are removed by the shell when you source the file.

checks.name: the variables do not leak
checks.fail: Source the file inside `( ... )`, a subshell, so its variables stay there.

hints: `f=${1:-/etc/os-release}` takes the argument or the default.
`( . "$f"; echo "$ID ${VERSION_ID:--}" )`: `${VERSION_ID:--}` means "VERSION_ID, or `-` when it is empty".
With `set -u`, an unset `VERSION_ID` is an error; `${VERSION_ID:--}` handles it.
solution: # osinfo [FILE]: prints "ID VERSION_ID" from an os-release file (default /etc/os-release).
explain: Sourcing is the documented way to read `os-release` on the machine itself. For files **collected from other machines**,
remember that sourcing runs them as code: if you do not trust where they came from, parse them instead

steps.title: Which family is it?
prompt: Runbooks branch on the distro **family**, not on every distro. Write `~/bin/osfamily [FILE]` that prints `debian`,
`rhel`, `suse`, `arch`, `alpine` or `unknown`. Look at `ID` first, then each word of `ID_LIKE` in order, and print the
Linux Mint has `ID=linuxmint` and `ID_LIKE="ubuntu debian"`, so it is `debian`. Test on `~/fleet/*/os-release`.

checks.name: this machine is debian
checks.fail: `~/bin/osfamily` with no argument should print `debian` (it reads `/etc/os-release`). Is it executable?

checks.name: every fleet host gets the right family
checks.cmd: while read -r h want; do got=$(~/bin/osfamily ~/fleet/$h/os-release 2>/dev/null); [ "$got" = "$want" ] || { echo "$h: got '$got', want '$want'"; exit 1; }; done < /opt/dojo/state/families
checks.fail: A host gets the wrong family (below). Check `ID` first, then each word of `ID_LIKE`.

checks.name: an unknown distro is unknown
checks.cmd: f=$(mktemp); printf 'ID=plan9\nVERSION_ID=4\n' > "$f"; got=$(~/bin/osfamily "$f" 2>/dev/null); rm -f "$f"; test "$got" = unknown
checks.fail: A file with `ID=plan9` and no `ID_LIKE` should give `unknown`.

hints: Read both fields in a subshell: `read -r id like < <(ID= ID_LIKE=; . "$f"; echo "$ID $ID_LIKE")`. `like` gets all remaining words.
Loop over the words: `for w in $id $like; do case $w in debian|ubuntu) echo debian; exit ;; ... esac; done; echo unknown`.
`opensuse*` in a `case` pattern matches `opensuse-leap` and `opensuse-tumbleweed`. `${w,,}` lowercases a value.
solution: # osfamily [FILE]: the distro family, from ID and then the words of ID_LIKE.
for f in ~/fleet/*/os-release; do echo "$f $(~/bin/osfamily "$f")"; done
steps.explain: `ID_LIKE` exists for exactly this: a derivative lists the distros it behaves like, closest first, so tools can support Mint, Rocky or Pop!_OS without knowing them by name. Install scripts (Docker's, NodeSource's) and configuration tools branch the same way.
